XA01.why: Not cited. Pens sold singly or in packs of 10; Leo needs at least 37 pens; least amount he can spend. Same mechanism (cover 'at least N' units with package options at least cost, comparing overshoot vs exact-fit combinations) and same ask (least dollars). Two box sizes instead of single vs pack, and here exact fit beats overshoot (reverse of 149), but that is a numbers change. Cross-exam re-skin. Drop.
Cited. Maximize profit under a ceiling. Different objective and constraint direction.
Not cited. 3- and 5-point questions, at most 20 answered, at least 80 points, least number of 5-point questions. Integer covering constraint, different ask.

XA02.why: Cited. y-intercept after a horizontal translation of a parabola. Line in standard form with both shifts here. Agree close.
Cited. Vertical shift run back to a slope. Different ask.
Not cited. f(x) + 3 is the same line as f(x + 2), find the slope. Same 'horizontal shift changes a line by slope x shift' fact, different ask. Keep apart.

XA03.why: Cited. Absolute-value equation with an extraneous root. Different.

XA04.why: Not cited. y − 50 = 4(x − 10); best interpretation of 50 = 'the number of members 10 weeks after the club was formed'. Same mechanism (model in point-slope form, so the constant is the output at the shifted input, not the y-intercept) and same ask (interpret that constant), with the same trap (reading it as the value at 0). Drop.
Not cited. Plumber C = 65h + 90, interpret 90. Same context and same ask in slope-intercept form; with 000412 this makes XA04 a re-skin.

XA05.why: Not cited. x + y = 10, x − y = k; the solution satisfies x > 2y; least integer k. Same 'solve the system in terms of k, then impose a condition on (x, y)' frame; the ask here is an equation, not an inequality. Allowed; keep apart.

XA06.why: Cited. Vertex of two constraints. Different.

Not cited. 3 cups of flour and 2 eggs per batch with 10 cups and 8 eggs; greatest number of batches. Same 'each resource gives its own cap; the smaller one binds' key step, with a flour context. XA06 adds the fixed y and the system form. Allowed; cite it.

Same mechanism: turn a point on a transformed graph into a point on f, then use two points of f. XA07 uses f(2x) (horizontal compression) and asks f(0) (one more step). Borderline close; cite it and keep apart. If AA09 is ever drafted, keep only one.
Not cited. Point (2, 5) on f, which point is on −f(2x) + 1. The reverse direction of the same point mapping. Different ask.

XA08.why: Cited. Net rate with both rates given. Different.
Cited. Fill and empty times. Different.
Not cited. Piecewise heating and cooling rates. Different context and ask.

Not cited. Bike rental per-hour charge plus a fee (expression). Different ask.

XA10.why: Not cited. 3 hooks + 2 hinges + 1 latch = $11.20 and 1 + 2 + 3 = $8.80; total cost of one of each. Same coefficient pattern (1, 2, 3 / 3, 2, 1), same mechanism (add the equations to get 4(s + m + l)) and same ask (one of each), with only the context and totals changed. Not cited. Add the equations to isolate a symmetric combination. Close.

XA11.why: Not cited. A line with slope 3 through the symbolic points (a, b) and (b, a + 6). Same symbolic-points slope frame; 603 is hard, XA11 is easy. Allowed.

Not cited. A line with slope −3/4 through (8, 1); y-intercept. The same slope and the same run of 8 give the same core computation ((3/4)(8) = 6). Change XA11's numbers (e.g. slope −2/5 with a run of 10, or slope 5/3 with a run of 6).

XA12.why: Not cited, and the nearest match. Table of values of linear f and g; for what x is f(x) = g(x). Same setup (two linear functions given by a table, find where they meet). XA12 gives only two points each, at non-zero x, and asks for the y-coordinate. Allowed because the ask differs; cite it and keep apart.

XA14.why: Not cited. XC01.why: Not cited, and the nearest match. P(junior | club) = P(club | junior); solve for a cell. The key insight is the same (equal numerators, so the row total must equal the column total). Here every cell is given and the student finds which pair qualifies. Different ask, so allowed, but the 'aha' is the same: cite it and keep it in a different batch from 826 (batch-075).

XC02.why: Not cited. 600 underclassmen and 400 upperclassmen; separate random samples of 60 and 80; 18 and 32 would join; best estimate of the school total (340), with the pooled-sample trap. Same mechanism (two groups sampled at unequal fractions, so each group's rate is scaled to its own size), same ask (estimated population count), and the same pooled and swapped-weight traps. Only the numbers and context change. The generator's own note ('distinct from household-weighted') misses this. Drop.

within_list_cues.XC03: Key cue: A is the only choice that brings in students outside the A group. B, C and D all describe only the 40 or 50 A students, so a test-wise student picks A because it is the only one with a comparison group. Revise one distractor to bring in a comparison group that does not answer the question, e.g. 'The percent of the students who earned an A in geometry who attended the tutoring program'. Do NOT use 'the percent of all students who attended tutoring': with the 80% it also answers the question (a second defensible key).
within_list_cues.XC04: Key C is the longest choice and the only hedged one ('may not reflect'); A, B and D are absolute. Shorten C (e.g. 'All inspected items come from machine D.') or hedge one distractor. No second defensible answer: A is false (A, B and C items have a 0 chance), and B is false (every 4th item is also D).
within_list_cues.XC05: Cue: the stem gives the 58-96°F range, and only the key D uses it, so the range is a given number that points straight to the key. D is also the longest choice. Revise to a 2x2 of (model prediction vs observed fact) x (within vs outside the data range), e.g. add 'The model predicts 0 iced drinks at about 22.9°F, a temperature within the range of the data' in place of B or C. C also gets the sign wrong in a way common sense eliminates (the y-intercept is −96, a negative count).
within_list_cues.XC06: None. Roman numeral I is in every choice, so the item reduces to deciding II and III. That is acceptable. The rationale's mean value is wrong (see math_errors).
within_list_cues.XC09: The 1.8 trap (15% of 12) has no tempting path. Acceptable for SPR; no cue.
within_list_cues.XC10: Choice-rationale problem: B's stated trap (dividing by the 2024 value) is impossible, because dividing by the new value never reorders percent increases (see math_errors). C's rationale ('a mix of size and change') is not a real error path. Key cue: the key (robotics) is the club with the smallest absolute increase, the classic 'trick' answer, so a test-wise student may pick it without computing. Revise B and C to real traps (e.g. B = the greatest 2024 percent of total membership; C = the greatest ratio of 2024 to 2022 members misread), or make the key a club whose absolute increase is not the smallest.

Reword the stem to 'Which of the following correctly describes the mean and median of the 8 remaining numbers?'

math_errors.none (keys): All 30 keys recomputed with sympy/fractions (scratchpad scr/verify29.py): XA01 54 (combos a=0..6: 56, 59, 55, 58, 54, 57, 60); XA02 −23/3 (A −5, B −7, D −7/3 check); XA03 x = 6, 2, sum 8; XA04 140 (value at h = 0 is 55); XA05 k = 14 (x = 8, y = 5); XA06 17 (caps 20 and 17; vertex 175/11); XA07 2 (traps −7, 29 check); XA08 24 (A 15, B 10; traps 38, 58/3 check); XA09 r = 15 (F = 10); XA10 s + m + l = 18 (one-parameter family s = l − 4, m = 22 − 2l); XA11 −6 (−32/3, −3/32); XA12 p = 5, q = 16 (midpoint trap 13); XA13 6 (trap 3/2); XA14 35t − 300, root 60/7; XA15 [1/5, 4] (numeric sweep confirms); XC01 only grade 11/band (totals 48/60/92 vs 60/70/70); XC02 4,680 (5,100, 5,520); XC05 96/4.2 = 22.86; XC06 median 1, mode 1; XC07 13:14 (7/15 trap); XC08 15.12 = 378/25 (2.16, 0.09); XC09 50; XC10 robotics 37.5%; XC11 mean 201/4 = 50.25, median 50 or 54 in examples; XC12 simulation confirms A; XC13 1600/31; XC14 2 (3.2); XC15 90 (45, 510).
math_errors.XC06: Rationale for choice C says that treating '4 or more' as exactly 4 gives a mean of 1.46. The correct figure is (0·12 + 1·15 + 2·11 + 3·7 + 4·5)/50 = 78/50 = 1.56.
math_errors.XC10: The claim that 'dividing by the new value instead of the original reorders the clubs', and B's rationale (robotics 9/33 ≈ 27% puts chess ahead), are false. By 2024 values: chess 23.1%, drama 19.4%, robotics 27.3%, debate 14.9%, so robotics is still greatest. Mathematically, (new − old)/new = 1 − old/new is an increasing function of new/old, exactly as (new − old)/old is, so the wrong base can never reorder increases. That trap cannot work as a choice rationale.
math_errors.XC13: Key 51.6 is a rounded repeating decimal (1600/31). The 61.5 trap is 0.8/1.3 = 61.538..., also repeating. Not an error in the key, but a format issue (see revise).
math_errors.XA08: Trap '19.33' = 58/3 is correct as computed, but it is a repeating decimal; it is only a trap, so this is fine.
